en: The Sūtra on the Elder’s Son Citta, Spoken by the Buddha, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master An Shigao of Parthia during the Later Han Dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Vulture Peak Mountain in Rājagṛha, together with [the assembly].
Five hundred śramaṇas, all of whom were arhats, together entered the city at dawn, wearing their kāṣāyas and carrying their alms bowls to beg for food.

At that time, there was in the city a family of the four castes that was the most noble and wealthy in the land; they dwelt on high and dry ground, and their residence featured excellent towers and pavilions, surrounded by walls seven layers deep with gates.
In a prominent family of the four castes named Tāṇḍyaka, there was a son named Śreṇika.
When he was sixteen years old, his father Tāṇḍyaka passed away; consequently, Śreṇika lived alone with his mother.
When the Buddha arrived at her house to beg for food, Cīrā was staying inside by the third gate. Seeing the Buddha approaching from afar, she thought to herself:
"How singularly handsome and exceptionally beautiful this man is!"
"He is as beautiful as a bright moon-jewel; his radiance is like that of the sun and moon; his complexion is like pure gold; he is like the full moon on the fifteenth day.
At that time, the Buddha was standing outside the gate, and the boy hurried inside and said to his mother:

"I saw a man coming who is so exceptionally handsome and peerless that there is no one like him in all the world. Since my birth, I have never seen anyone such as this; he is now standing at the gate wishing to beg for alms."
The mother of Jentī said, "You should beg for it.
Her mother was extremely stingy and greedy and refused to give it; Jentī spoke out:
"Mother, out of compassion for me, please grant this to this person;
to give it to this person is like a sick man obtaining a skilled physician.
Thus she spoke again.
"Whoever gives to this person, their name shall reach as far as the heavens above and the earth below; this person is currently staying outside.
His mother again refused to beg, yet he repeatedly urged her until she would not stop.
The mother became angry and said to Citta:
"If you do not stop harassing me, you will cause me great distress.
The mother spoke thus.
"This man did not come for the sake of begging; he merely wishes to deceive and provoke you.
You are but a small, foolish child—what do you know?
If you do not cease your demands, you shall surely receive a beating with my staff before you stop."
The Buddha, foreseeing that his mother was stingy and greedy, manifested his majestic spiritual power so that it penetrated and illuminated the interior of the seven-layered gates.
When Ciñcā saw the Buddha’s radiance, her heart was filled with great joy. She immediately returned to her mother’s side and addressed her, saying:
"Foolish woman, you do not know the merit of giving; you are like a blind man who has fallen into fire, existing only because he lacks eyes."
People of the world merely sit idly in stinginess and greed, refusing to believe in the merit of giving; they shall later reap its calamity.

When people harbor evil thoughts, speak evil words, and commit evil deeds with their bodies—being foolish, they do not believe in the Buddha, they do not believe in the Sūtras, and they do not believe in the Saṅgha of Bhikṣus—after death, they all fall into the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals.

If a person is not stingy or greedy, believes in giving, and later obtains its blessings; if they practice good through body, speak good through speech, and think good through mind, they will obtain blessings for themselves. Such a person’s household should always give, and by following wise people, one causes others to possess wisdom.
Cīra said:
"If my mother is unwilling to give it to me, bring me my portion of today's meal; I would rather go a day without food.
Bring it to me quickly out of pity, for I wish to give it to this person, fearing that he might abandon me."
"This person has abandoned me and left; such a person is difficult to encounter.

Her mother again refused to give them, so Cīra went herself to take her portion of the rice and also took the fine garment she was wearing. Carrying these away, she went to where the Buddha was, prostrated with her head at the Buddha’s feet, stood back with palms joined, and said to the Buddha:
"I offer all the clothing and food I possess; I pray that you accept them for the Buddha."
The Buddha remained silent and did not respond.
Jie addressed him again, saying:
“Now the Buddha is the Teacher of those above heaven and those below it among men; you should compassionately deliver us. We pray that you will accept this for our sake, so that we may obtain merit.”
When he had thus requested three times, the Buddha accepted it, and Citta was immediately filled with great joy.
The Buddha said to Citta:

"Now you have subdued all those who are stingy and greedy; today you have bestowed robes and food upon the Buddha, and whatever desires and aspirations you harbor in your heart shall likewise be fulfilled."
Filled with great joy, he again addressed the Buddha, saying:

"As for my aspiration, I do not seek to become Śakra, the King of the Second Heaven of the Trāyastriṃśa; nor do I seek to become Brahmā, the King of the Seventh Heaven; nor do I seek wealth and nobility in every lifetime. My only wish is that the radiance of my wisdom may be like that of the Buddha."
The Buddha said,
"Excellent! May all your aspirations be fulfilled."
On the second day, having heard the words of Citta, Śakra, King of Devas, stood behind the Buddha with palms joined. Then, before the Buddha, Śakra, King of Devas, spoke to Citta, saying:

"If you wish to seek Buddhahood by offering this small amount of food and clothing to the Buddha today, you shall not attain it; even after ten kalpas, a hundred kalpas, a thousand kalpas, ten thousand kalpas, or a hundred million kalpas, you will still not be able to become a Buddha."
The Restrainer replied to King Śakra:

"I do not wish to become a Buddha for the sake of even a single meal; rather, I shall always maintain a virtuous mind with diligent and tireless effort, seeking Buddhahood without ceasing, and I shall surely become a Buddha."
The Heavenly King Śakra replied to Zhi, saying:

"Even if you were to hold up Mount Sumeru made of the four jewels, and maintain a mind of loving-kindness toward the people of the world for thousands of millions and hundreds of millions of kalpas, you would still not yet be able to attain Buddhahood."
Śakra-devānām-indra replied again to the World-Governor:
"It is like a master carpenter who enters the mountains with an axe to seek timber; he must select and take only that which is fine and straight, and he takes only what is to his satisfaction."
"I do not seek to become a Buddha for the sake of even a single meal or a garment.
Śakra, King of Devas, spoke again to Jie, saying:

"If you wish to seek Buddhahood, it involves extreme suffering; it would be better for you to seek to become a Brahmā of the Seventh Heaven, or a Śakra, King of Devas, in the Second Heaven, Trāyastriṃśa. If you seek to become a Buddha, it is difficult to attain."
Śakra replied to the King of the Gods:
"Have you ever seen within Jambudvīpa?
Śakra, the King of the Gods, said:
"I see it. He made this vow:
"If a great fire fills it and rises up to heaven, I shall cast my body into it; I will resolutely seek to become a Buddha and never cease."
The Heavenly King Śakra said:

"Suppose you were to fill the entire land of Jambudvīpa with fire; within it dwell humans, animals, and even crawling insects—you must not kill them. Since your mouth speaks evil and your mind harbors evil thoughts, upon death you shall enter hell. How, then, can you become a Buddha?"
Śakra, King of Devas, replied to the Regulator:

"The people of the world and even the crawling insects—I entrust them all to Maitreya Buddha with a heart of loving-kindness. Maitreya Buddha shall himself deliver and liberate them; as for me, my pursuit of the Buddha-way shall never cease."
Brahmā Śikhin replied again to King Śakra:
"The abodes of the seventh Brahmakāyika devas and the second King Śakra must inevitably decline; all shall return to death, and there is none who can escape it."
Śakra, King of Devas, then joined his palms and replied to Jie, saying:
"Your resolve is as firm as this; if you continue to seek Buddhahood without ceasing, you shall certainly become a Buddha."
Śibi replied again to Śakra, King of Devas:

"Do not harbor the conceit of your celestial mind and be self-exalting; there are those who surpass you. I maintain a virtuous mind and practice with diligence without slackening, seeking Buddhahood without ceasing; I shall certainly attain Buddhahood."
Śakra, King of Devas, remained silent and said nothing further. The Buddha then addressed Ciñcā:

“Throughout your past and present lives, you have served sixty thousand Buddhas. You should always vow to seek Buddhahood; you must always maintain a mind of diligent effort in serving the Buddhas. After two hundred billion kalpas, you shall no longer be reborn among hell-beings, hungry ghosts, or animals. When those two hundred billion kalpas have passed, you shall become a Cakravartin King, over whom ten billion small kingdoms will be subordinate; you shall rule over the four continents and possess the power of flight.”

Your conduct shall be upright; when your life ends, you shall ascend to be born in the seventh Brahmā Heaven and the fourth Tuṣita Heaven. When your lifespan in those heavens ends, you shall descend again to be born as a Cakravartin King. When that life ends, you shall again ascend to be born in the seventh Brahmā Heaven.

When these hundred billion myriad kalpas of ascending and descending have ended, you shall become a Buddha named Sumerukāla; you shall deliver and liberate the people of the heavens above and the world below. When you are born into this lower realm, you shall illuminate twelve thousand billion worlds of heaven and earth, reaching upward as far as the twenty-eighth heaven. Heaven and earth will all tremble greatly; the night will be as bright as the rising sun, and the lifespan of the people shall be seven thousand billion years.

Your body shall be two hundred zhang in height; there shall be eleven thousand cities, each city four hundred and eighty li in size, all of which shall be constructed with wooden planks and adorned with the seven treasures—gold, silver, lapis lazuli, crystal, coral, musaragalva, and agate—engraved and inlaid.
"When you become a Buddha, you shall preach the sutras on two occasions. At the first assembly, six thousand *koṭis* of śramaṇas will all attain arhatship;
at the second assembly when you preach the sutras, four thousand *koṭis* of śramaṇas will all attain arhatship."

At that time, among the people there were no thieves; men and women were all of one mind, free from evil. There were no mountains, forests, streams, or valleys, for the earth was entirely level and even. The people were free from disease, sorrow, and suffering, and all lived in peace and happiness, each guarding their own dwelling.

Heaven sends rain three times a day, which just suffices to settle the dust; when people wish to converse, they all gather in great assemblies; in the summer months there is no heat, and in the winter months there is no cold, such that all attain a state of moderate comfort.

“The vihāra you instruct is named Nandita. If there are men or women who maintain the precepts and practice giving to Buddhas, Pratyekabuddhas, or Arhats, and seek to become Buddhas, they shall all attain Buddhahood.”

The Way must be sought; throughout the eight directions and above and below, there is none who can fathom its limits. Such is the wisdom of the Buddha: the people of the world do not know whence they come into life, nor do they know to what path they will go at death.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, Jeta and the assembly of bhikṣus all bowed their heads at the Buddha’s feet in prostration, paid their respects, and departed.
This concludes the Sutra on Jeta, the Son of a Householder, spoken by the Buddha.
